summary: Defines naming and structuring guidelines for X.500 directory pilots, focused on white pages. Following them is recommended so pilots work together. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives directory managers advice for organizing X.500 white pages. It recommends clear names and a structure that supports searching across separate pilot projects.

questions: what is a directory information tree
how should organisations be named in x.500
subtitle: Naming and structuring advice for X.500 white pages directory pilots.

tldr.problem: Separate X.500 directory pilots need consistent structures and names so users and software can search them reliably.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends a shallow directory tree, meaningful names with alternative values for abbreviations, and consistent use of attributes and language values.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational guidance for directory pilots and obsoletes RFC 1384. It does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1617 is an Informational memo published in May 1994 that obsoletes RFC 1384. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Audience and Scope
sections.content:
The guidelines are for data managers using X.500 Directory Services. They focus on white pages, where users search for people and organizations, and help managers choose the directory tree structure and the information stored for each entry.

The RFC assumes use of the COSINE and Internet X.500 schema. It recommends that directory pilots follow the guidance but does not define an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This guide is for people who manage an X.500 directory. It helps them decide where entries belong and which information to store.

sections.title: A Shallow Directory Tree
sections.content:
The suggested tree places countries and selected international organizations near its root, with organizations, localities, organizational units, people, and roles below. International organizations may appear directly under the root; multinational companies are represented under country or locality entries.

For white pages, the RFC recommends keeping the tree as flat as possible because users are expected to search by name rather than browse through many levels. Even large organizations should need no more than two organizational-unit levels, and smaller organizations should consider using none.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the directory tree broad and shallow so names stay short and people can search for entries. Use organizational units only when they help distinguish entries.

sections.title: Representing Multinational Organizations
sections.content:
The X.500 structure described in the RFC places multinational organizations below country or locality entries. The document outlines three ways to connect their parts: one organization tree with aliases in each country, separate country entries linked by aliases, or separate subtrees connected by an attribute such as seeAlso.

The first two approaches can let directory operations follow the links. With loosely linked subtrees, a user interface must choose to follow the references. Each approach affects how natural the names look and what views of the organization users can search.
sections.plainLanguage: A multinational can use one main entry with aliases, separate national entries linked together, or separate entries with references between them. The links affect how users search across the organization.

sections.title: Names That Support Searching
sections.content:
Names should be unique and easy to query. The RFC recommends using full organization names in relative distinguished names, such as University College London, and storing abbreviations as additional values so searches can still find them.

For people, use a common form of the person's name and keep alternative forms as additional values. When names collide, use extra attributes such as a title, room number, or user ID rather than adding an arbitrary number to the name. National naming guidance should generally be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a clear full name as the main directory name and store familiar abbreviations as extra search values. Add a meaningful detail when two entries would otherwise have the same name.

sections.title: Attribute Values and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC recommends using attribute values as the standards define them. Because the directory standard at the time lacked language support, an entry could have multiple values in local languages and English. Where a character set might not display for users, the RFC recommends adding a transliterated value.

The object class and naming attributes should normally be publicly readable so searches can work, unless an entry is intended to be private. The memo says security issues are not substantially discussed and warns that a directory password should not be reused as a system password if others might read it.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra language or transliterated values can help people find names they cannot type in the main character set. The memo gives little security guidance and warns against reusing a system password.
